title: Words That Bookend Later Words
statement:
You get a list of lowercase strings words. Say that a word a bookends a word b when b both starts with a and ends with a. The two copies of a may overlap inside b, and a word always bookends an identical word.

Count the index pairs (i, j) with i < j where words[i] bookends words[j]. Note the direction: only an earlier word can bookend a later one.

examples.why: "ab" bookends "abcab" and the second "ab". "aba" starts with "ab" but ends with "ba", so it does not count.
The first "a" bookends the three words after it. "aa" also bookends "aaa": the two copies share the middle letter, and overlap is allowed.
"x" would bookend "xyzx", but it comes later in the list. Only pairs with the shorter word first count.

hints: With at most 50 words, checking every pair (i, j) with i < j is perfectly fine. What exactly do you check for one pair?
For a pair, words[j] must start with words[i] and end with words[i]. A word longer than words[j] can never pass.

Faster for long lists: walk left to right with a count of the words seen so far. For the current word, try every length L where its first L letters equal its last L letters, and add how many earlier words equal that piece.

explain.intuition:
The rule is just two checks on a pair: b.startsWith(a) and b.endsWith(a). With 50 words there are about 1 200 pairs, so the direct double loop is the intended answer. The only traps are the direction (only i < j) and remembering that overlapping copies are fine, which both string methods handle on their own.

If the list were long, flip the question around. For the current word b, which strings could bookend it? Only its prefixes that are also its suffixes, and a word of length 10 has at most 10 of those. Keep a hash map counting the words already seen, and for each such "border" of b, add the count. That is O(total length²) instead of O(n²).
steps: Start a counter at 0 and an empty map from word to how many times it has appeared so far.
For each word b in order, try every length L from 1 to b.length.
If the first L letters equal the last L letters, add the map's count for that piece to the answer.
Then add b itself to the map, so it can bookend words that come after it.
pitfalls: Counting both directions. A later short word that matches an earlier long word does not count: ["xyzx", "x"] gives 0.
Adding the current word to the map before checking it. Then every word would count as bookending itself.
Rejecting overlap by checking that the word is at least twice as long. "aa" bookends "aaa".

complexity.time: O(n² · m) for the pair check, O(n · m²) with the map

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: For each i < j, test whether words[j] starts and ends with words[i].

solutions.title: Count earlier words, look up each border
solutions.idea: Only a prefix of b that is also a suffix of b can bookend it. Look each such piece up in a count of the words seen so far.

followups: There are 100 000 words with total length 500 000. The map version builds many substrings; how would a trie keyed on (prefix letter, suffix letter) pairs avoid that?
How would you find, for a single word, all lengths where its prefix equals its suffix in O(m) instead of O(m²)? (Think of the failure table in KMP.)
lcTitle: Count Prefix and Suffix Pairs I
